input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-589: Undergraduate Thesis Proposal and Preparation. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: Students work with a supervising faculty member to complete their undergraduate thesis proposal, and do additional background preparation (e.g., programming, study, exercises, and analysis) for the subject area and specific problem(s) to be addressed in a thesis. At the end of the semester, a thesis proposal must be submitted for approval to the advisor. Additional deliverables set by the advisor are also required (e.g., source code, bibliographies, notes, presentations, etc.). Contact Hours: Independent Study 1 Typically Offered: Fall

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-589]
Students work with a supervising faculty member to complete their undergraduate thesis proposal, and do additional background preparation (e.g., programming, study, exercises, and analysis) for the subject area and specific problem(s) to be addressed in a thesis. At the end of the semester, a thesis proposal must be submitted for approval to the advisor. Additional deliverables set by the advisor are also required (e.g., source code, bibliographies, notes, presentations, etc.). Contact Hours: Independent Study 1 Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: Students work with a supervising faculty member to complete their undergraduate thesis proposal, and do additional background preparation for the subject area and specific problem.
beats.example: A student collaborates with their advisor to draft a proposal that outlines a machine learning project on educational data analysis.
beats.title: Introduction to Thesis Preparation
beats.visualDirection: Display a simple flowchart showing the sequence: Advisor Consultation -> Background Preparation -> Proposal Drafting -> Advisor Review.

beats.claim: A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, and defines a reproducible method to address specific problems.
beats.example: Students transform a broad interest in 'AI ethics' into a focused question about 'bias detection in automated grading tools.'
beats.title: Defining the Research Problem
beats.visualDirection: Show a Venn diagram comparing broad interests, literature gaps, and a clearly defined research question.

beats.claim: Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work and ensure reproducibility.
beats.example: Students document exact software versions, dataset sources, and step-by-step procedures for their thesis experiment.
beats.title: Methodology and Reproducibility
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a checklist template with fields for 'Dataset Source', 'Code Repository', 'Parameter Settings', and 'Reproduction Steps'.

beats.claim: Computing professionals should be honest and trustworthy, avoid harm, and respect privacy and confidentiality.
beats.example: Students include a section in their proposal detailing how they will anonymize student data and obtain necessary permissions.
beats.title: Ethical Computing Standards
beats.visualDirection: Present a side-by-side comparison of 'Ethical Compliance' vs. 'Potential Harm' with checkmarks for privacy, fairness, and transparency.

beats.claim: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence and cites prior work to identify contributions.
beats.example: Students structure their proposal to clearly separate their novel hypothesis from established literature findings.
beats.title: Responsible Technical Communication
beats.visualDirection: Show a two-column layout: 'Claim' (student's contribution) vs. 'Evidence' (prior research citations), with arrows linking them.

beats.claim: Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion, and limitations should be made visible.
beats.example: Students draft a subsection explicitly stating potential biases in their dataset and how they will validate their findings.
beats.title: Results and Limitations
beats.visualDirection: Create a template box labeled 'Limitations & Threats to Validity' with prompts for data constraints, methodological gaps, and mitigation strategies.

beats.claim: Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification.
beats.example: Students use citation management tools to track all references and verify that all code and data are properly attributed.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Plagiarism
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart: 'Source Identification' -> 'Citation Formatting' -> 'Plagiarism Check' -> 'Integrity Verification'.

beats.claim: Additional deliverables set by the advisor are also required, such as source code, bibliographies, notes, and presentations.
beats.example: Students create a project management tracker that logs weekly milestones for coding, literature review, and draft presentations.
beats.title: Supervisor Deliverables and Planning
beats.visualDirection: Show a Gantt chart template with phases: 'Proposal Draft', 'Code Setup', 'Literature Review', 'Advisor Feedback', 'Final Submission'.

beats.claim: Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products, and maintain high standards of professional competence.
beats.example: Students apply a rubric that scores their proposal on clarity, methodological rigor, ethical compliance, and alignment with advisor goals.
beats.title: Evaluation Criteria and Quality Standards
beats.visualDirection: Present a scoring matrix with categories: 'Problem Definition', 'Methodology', 'Ethics', 'Communication', and 'Feasibility' with 1-5 scales.

beats.claim: Students must submit a thesis proposal for approval to the advisor at the end of the semester, ensuring all components are complete and compliant.
beats.example: Students run a final review against a checklist: problem statement, literature review, reproducible methods, ethical considerations, citations, and advisor deliverables.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a printable checklist template with checkboxes for each requirement, a signature line for advisor approval, and a submission deadline field.

learningObjectives: Students will articulate the core components of a thesis proposal, including problem definition, methodology, and evaluation criteria.
Students will demonstrate how to integrate ACM ethical guidelines and responsible research communication standards into their proposal development.
Students will produce a structured proposal outline that aligns with supervisor requirements and academic integrity standards.
